newsitem.title: USA: U.S. EPA boiler proposal would boost natgas demand.
newsitem.headline: U.S. EPA boiler proposal would boost natgas demand.

text.p: A U.S. plan to set tight limits on emissions from new utility and industrial boilers could boost natural gas demand by 200 to 300 billion cubic feet a year by 2010, a natural gas group said Wednesday.

The Environmental Protection Agency Tuesday completed a proposal to set a 1.35 pounds per megawatt-hour limit on emissions of nitrogen oxides (NOx) from new boilers, based on 0.15 pounds of NOx per million British thermal units.

In contrast, the standard for existing boilers is based not on efficiency or output, but on the fuel used, ranging from a high of 0.6 pounds per million Btu for coal to a low of 0.2 pounds per million Btu for natural gas.
Gas industry groups had pressed for the fuel-neutral standard, which they said would help correct biases in favor of coal in the Clean Air Act.

Bruce Craig, environmental director for the Natural Gas Supply Association said if the Clean Air Act in 1990 had been written with fuel-neutral standards, U.S. power producers today would be burning 2 to 3 trillion cubic feet more natural gas annually than the 13 Tcf they use today.

Utilities that depend on cheap coal had expected the tight new emissions limits, but were surprised that the EPA proposal included an efficiency standard, and concerned that EPA had defined new boilers to include existing boilers that were being modified or reconstructed.

"The main concern is to minimize the cases where a unit is somehow modified and somehow gets pulled into possibly having to meet these new source performance standards," said John Kinsman, manager of atmospheric science at the Edison Electric Institute, which represents investor-owned utilities.
"It's a very strict standard," he said.
